The proposed framework uses composite potential fields to balance exploration, pursuit responsiveness, and natural guard behavior.
The information field guides guards towards potential areas of interest.
The confidence field discourages immediate re-visits to already covered areas.
The connectivity field prioritizes or de-prioritizes structural features based on their weights.
The kernel-filtered decision process combines the three individual fields into a single potential.
The Capture Experiment assesses short-term pursuit efficiency under heightened difficulty.
The Fixed-Time Experiment measures long-term patrol stability in a standard setting.
Five guard control modes are evaluated: Potential Field, Random Walk, Finite State Machine, Staleness-based FSM, and Cheat.
Two player-control strategies are implemented: MaxMin and SafetyGraph.
The staleness metric grows with time since its last visit, driving guards toward under-patrolled areas.
The kernel-smoothed potential is a weighted average of the composite potential over all nodes within a certain radius.
The lookahead threshold balances foresight and computational cost, typically set to 2-3 times the average inter-node distance.
The spatial decay factor controls the decay of the composite potential with distance, typically set to 0.1.
The temporal decay rate controls the decay of the information and confidence fields over time, typically set to 0.9.
The maximum duration used in the Capture Experiment is 60 seconds.
The fixed duration used in the Fixed-Time Experiment is 60 seconds.
The proposed framework is evaluated on five representative game maps, two player-control policies, and five guard modes.
The results show that the proposed framework outperforms classical baseline methods in both capture efficiency and patrol naturalness.
